cards.title: A cryptarithm is a mathematical puzzle where digits in an arithmetic operation…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: A cryptarithm is a mathematical puzzle where digits in an arithmetic operation (addition, subtraction, multiplication, division) are replaced by letters or symbols; each letter represents a unique digit (0-9), and the same letter always represents the same digit throughout the puzzle. Solving a cryptarithm requires algebraic reasoning — translating column-by-column arithmetic into equations with unknowns and using place value, carry logic, and digit constraints to deduce each letter's value.
steps: Imagine you receive a coded message: SEND + MORE = MONEY
Each letter hides a digit
Where do you start? Begin with the column that gives you the most information — the leftmost column
In MONEY, the M must come from a carry (since SEND and MORE are both 4-digit numbers, their sum is at most 5 digits)
So M = 1 (carry from the thousands column)
Now look at the thousands column: S + E + carry = O + 10 × (carry to ten-thousands)
cards.misconception: A wrong answer like "C can be any digit" reveals the student has not applied the constraint that the maximum sum of two two-digit numbers is 198, missing the bounding logic that forces C = 1.
remember: In the cryptarithm AB + BA = CDC, why must C be 1.
In the cryptarithm ONE + ONE = TWO, if O = 2, find T and explain your reasoning.
Why can the leading letter of any number in a cryptarithm never represent 0.

cards.title: A natural number N can be expressed as a sum of two or more consecutive natural…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: A natural number N can be expressed as a sum of two or more consecutive natural numbers if there exist integers k ≥ 2 (number of terms) and a ≥ 1 (first term) such that N = a + (a+1) + ... + (a+k-1) = k·a + k(k-1)/2. This representation is possible exactly when N has an odd divisor greater than 1, or equivalently, when N is not a power of 2.
steps: Imagine you have ₹50 and want to give it to a group of children such that each child gets ₹1 more than the previous child, and every child gets at least ₹1
How many children can you have, and how much does the first child get? This is exactly writing 50 as a sum of consecutive numbers
We start by recalling from c8_math_ch5_1 that the sum of k consecutive numbers starting from a is k·a + k(k-1)/2
We set this equal to 50 and try different values of k (number of children) to see which give a positive integer a
The key insight is that 2N = k(2a + k - 1), so k must be a divisor of 2N, and (2N/k - k + 1) must be even and positive
We systematically test each divisor k of 2N that is ≥ 2.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer like k·a + k(k+1)/2 or just k·a reveals the student does not remember the correct formula for the sum of an arithmetic series with difference 1, or confuses it with the sum of first k natural numbers.
remember: What is the algebraic expression for the sum of k consecutive natural numbers starting from a.
Explain why the number 16 cannot be written as a sum of two or more consecutive natural numbers.
Find all ways to write 21 as a sum of consecutive natural numbers. Show your working.

cards.title: An odd number can always be expressed as the sum of two consecutive integers.
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: An odd number can always be expressed as the sum of two consecutive integers. Specifically, for any integer \(n \ge 1\), the odd number \(2n+1 = n + (n+1)\). The two consecutive numbers are \(\frac{O-1}{2}\) and \(\frac{O+1}{2}\) where \(O\) is the given odd number.
steps: Imagine Rohan has 11 marbles and wants to split them into two piles such that one pile has exactly one more marble than the other
Can he do it? Let the smaller pile be \(x\) marbles, then the larger pile is \(x+1\)
Together they have \(x + (x+1) = 2x+1 = 11\)
Solving gives \(2x=10\), so \(x=5\)
The piles are 5 and 6
This connects to Class 7 parity rules: one of two consecutive numbers is always even, the other odd, so their sum is always odd
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (even) reveals the student does not recall the parity property of consecutive numbers – that one must be even and the other odd, and even + odd = odd.
remember: State the rule: The sum of two consecutive numbers is always ______ (even/odd).
Explain why the sum of two consecutive numbers is always odd. Use the concept of even and odd numbers in your explanation.
Find the two consecutive numbers whose sum is 47.

cards.title: An even number can be expressed as a sum of two or more consecutive natural…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: An even number can be expressed as a sum of two or more consecutive natural numbers if and only if it is not a power of 2 (i.e., it has at least one odd factor greater than 1). The number of ways to write an even number as such a sum equals the number of odd divisors of that number minus 1.
steps: Imagine your class is arranging 24 chairs in a triangular formation where each row has one more chair than the row in front
Can you do it? Yes: 7+8+9 = 24
Now try with 32 chairs
Students test small even numbers (6, 10, 12, 14, 18, 20) and find representations, but 2, 4, 8, 16, 32 fail
Connect to c8_math_ch5_3: odd numbers always work as sum of two consecutive numbers
For even numbers, we need three or more terms
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., picking 18) reveals the student thinks all even numbers work or confuses the pattern with odd numbers.
remember: Which of the following even numbers CANNOT be expressed as a sum of two or more consecutive natural numbers: 18, 22, 32, 36.
Explain why 10 can be written as a sum of consecutive numbers (1+2+3+4) but 8 cannot, even though both are even.
Find a sum of consecutive natural numbers that equals 44. Show your steps.

cards.title: Parity rules state that the sum or difference of two integers follows…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: Parity rules state that the sum or difference of two integers follows predictable patterns based on whether each integer is even (divisible by 2) or odd (not divisible by 2): even ± even = even, odd ± odd = even, even ± odd = odd, and odd ± even = odd. These rules hold for all integers, including negative numbers and zero.
steps: Imagine you're at a kirana store with ₹500 and you buy items costing ₹127, ₹89, and ₹144
Without adding them up, can you tell if you'll have an even or odd amount of change left? This is where parity rules help
Start by recalling that even numbers are multiples of 2 (2k) and odd numbers are one more than a multiple of 2 (2k+1)
Write down the parity of each price: 127 (odd), 89 (odd), 144 (even)
Now apply the rules step by step: odd + odd = even, then even + even = even
The total spent is even
cards.misconception: A wrong answer reveals the student either doesn't recall the four basic parity rules, misidentifies negative numbers' parity (e.g., thinks −53 is even because 53 is odd), or incorrectly applies subtraction rules (treating a − b as a + b without considering…
remember: State the parity (even or odd) of each expression without calculating the actual sum or difference: (a) 347 + 582, (b) 419 − 276, (c) (−53) + (−88), (d) (−104) − (−37).
Explain why the sum of two odd numbers is always even, using the algebraic forms 2k+1 and 2m+1. Why does this proof work for negative odd numbers like −7 and −11 as well.
Three integers a, b, c have the following parities: a is even, b is odd, c is….

cards.title: Given four consecutive integers \(n, n+1, n+2, n+3\)…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: Given four consecutive integers \(n, n+1, n+2, n+3\), placing plus or minus signs between them creates an expression of the form \(n \pm (n+1) \pm (n+2) \pm (n+3)\) where each \(\pm\) is independently chosen as \(+\) or \(-\). The value of such an expression depends on the pattern of signs chosen, and the set of all possible values follows specific parity and range patterns determined by the starting number \(n\).
steps: Imagine you have four consecutive locker numbers: 12, 13, 14, 15

Your teacher asks: "If you put plus or minus signs between them in every possible way, what different totals can you get?" Start by writing the four numbers with boxes for signs: \(12 \square 13 \square 14 \square 15\)
Since there are 3 gaps and each can be \(+\) or \(-\), there are \(2^3 = 8\) combinations
Connect this to Class 7's parity rules (c7_math_ch06_003) — the sum/difference of integers follows even/odd patterns
Work through one example completely, then organize all 8 in a table to spot the pattern: all results are even (or all odd), and they form a symmetric set around the sum of the four numbers.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer of 6 or 4 reveals the student thinks some sign combinations are invalid or they are counting only distinct results rather than distinct expressions. A wrong answer of 16 reveals they think there are 4 gaps instead of 3.
remember: For the four consecutive numbers 5, 6, 7, 8, how many different expressions can be formed by placing + or - signs in the three gaps between them.
Consider the expression \(n - (n+1) + (n+2) - (n+3)\). Without substituting a specific value for \(n\), explain why the result must always be an even number.
For the consecutive numbers 10, 11, 12, 13, find the value of the expression with signs: \(10 - 11 - 12 + 13\). Then list all 8 possible values for this set of four numbers.

cards.title: Algebraic Explanation of Parity Patterns uses variables to represent even…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: Algebraic Explanation of Parity Patterns uses variables to represent even numbers as \(2k\) and odd numbers as \(2k+1\) (where \(k\) is any integer) to prove general rules about the parity (evenness or oddness) of sums, differences, and products. This algebraic representation shows why patterns observed with specific numbers hold true for all integers.
steps: Imagine a teacher asks: "Rohan has some ₹10 coins and some ₹5 coins
He says no matter how many of each he takes, the total will always be a multiple of 5
How can we prove this without checking every combination?" This is like proving parity patterns: we need a general argument
Start by recalling Class 7 parity rules (even+odd=odd, etc.)
Then introduce the algebraic forms: any even number is \(2 \times \text{integer}\), any odd is \(2 \times \text{integer} + 1\)
Write two even numbers as \(2a\) and \(2b\)
cards.misconception: A wrong answer like "even = \(2n\), odd = \(2n-1\)" is also algebraically correct but less standard; the key is recognizing \(n\) represents any…
remember: Write the algebraic form for an even number and an odd number using a variable \(n\). Explain what \(n\) represents.
Why does the algebraic proof for "odd + odd = even" use two different variables, like \(2a+1\) and \(2b+1\), instead of the same variable \(2n+1\) and \(2n+1\).
Prove algebraically that the product of an even number and an odd number is always even. Use \(2m\) for the even number and \(2n+1\) for the odd number.

cards.title: Divisibility tests are shortcut rules that determine whether a given integer is…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: Divisibility tests are shortcut rules that determine whether a given integer is divisible by another integer (2, 3, 5, 9, 10) without performing long division. Each test uses a specific property of the number's digits: for 2, 5, and 10, only the last digit matters; for 3 and 9, the sum of all digits must be a multiple of 3 or 9 respectively.
steps: Imagine your teacher has 1,235 candies and wants to distribute them equally among 2, 3, 5, 9, or 10 students without breaking any candy
How can you quickly check which group sizes work? Start by recalling from Class 6 (c6_math_ch01_014) that divisibility means the remainder is zero
Write the number 1,235 and observe its last digit (5) and sum of digits (1+2+3+5=11)
Connect this to place value: 1,235 = 1×1000 + 2×100 + 3×10 + 5
Since 10, 100, 1000 are all multiples of 2, 5, and 10, only the last digit decides divisibility by those numbers
For 3 and 9, note that 10 = 9+1, 100 = 99+1, etc., so the remainder depends on the sum of digits
remember: State the divisibility rule for 9 and give an example of a 3-digit number that is divisible by 9.
Why does the divisibility test for 3 work? Explain using the number 471 as an illustration.
Check whether 6,840 is divisible by 2, 3, 5, 9, and 10. Show your reasoning for each.

cards.title: Divisibility tests are shortcut rules to determine if a whole number is…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: Divisibility tests are shortcut rules to determine if a whole number is divisible by another without performing full division. For 4: a number is divisible by 4 if its last two digits form a number divisible by 4. For 6: a number must be divisible by both 2 and 3. For 8: a number is divisible by 8 if its last three digits form a number divisible by 8. For 11: a number is divisible by 11 if the difference between the sum of digits in odd positions and the sum of digits in even positions is either 0 or a multiple of 11.
steps: Imagine you have ₹2,376 and want to split it equally among 4 friends without doing long division
You notice the last two digits are 76, and since 76 ÷ 4 = 19, you know it divides evenly
This works because 100 is divisible by 4, so only the last two digits matter
For 6, you check if the number is even (divisible by 2) and if the digit sum is a multiple of 3
For 8, since 1000 is divisible by 8, only the last three digits matter
For 11, the alternating sum pattern emerges from the fact that 10 ≡ -1 (mod 11), so powers of 10 alternate between 1 and -1
remember: State the divisibility rule for 8 and give an example of a 5-digit number that is divisible by 8.
Why does the divisibility rule for 4 only require checking the last two digits? Explain using place value.
Is 53,292 divisible by 6? Show your work using the divisibility rules for 2 and 3.

cards.title: The distributive property of multiplication over addition states that for any…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: The distributive property of multiplication over addition states that for any three numbers \(a\), \(b\), and \(c\) (integers, fractions, decimals, or algebraic terms), multiplying \(a\) by the sum of \(b\) and \(c\) gives the same result as multiplying \(a\) by \(b\) and \(a\) by \(c\) separately, then adding the products: \(a \times (b + c) = a \times b + a \times c\).
steps: Imagine you are buying supplies for your classroom: each student needs 1 notebook (₹12) and 1 pen (₹8)
If there are 5 students, you can calculate the total cost in two ways
First, find the cost per student (₹12 + ₹8 = ₹20) and multiply by 5 (5 × 20 = ₹100)
Second, multiply the quantity of each item by 5 separately (5 × 12 = 60, 5 × 8 = 40) and add (60 + 40 = 100)
Both give ₹100
This is the distributive property: \(5 \times (12 + 8) = 5 \times 12 + 5 \times 8\)
cards.misconception: A wrong answer like \(a(b + c) = ab + c\) reveals the student thinks the multiplier only applies to the first term inside the bracket, a classic "incomplete distribution…
remember: State the distributive property of multiplication over addition using the variables \(a\), \(b\), and \(c\).
Explain why \(4 \times (3 + 5)\) and \(4 \times 3 + 4 \times 5\) give the same answer. Use the meaning of multiplication as repeated addition in your explanation.
Simplify \(7 \times \left(\frac{2}{3} + \frac{1}{6}\right)\) using the distributive property. Show all steps.

cards.title: The distributive property states that multiplying a sum by a number gives the…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: The distributive property states that multiplying a sum by a number gives the same result as multiplying each addend separately and then adding the products. An area model visualizes this by representing the product (a + b)(c + d) as the area of a rectangle with sides (a + b) and (c + d), which can be partitioned into four smaller rectangles of areas ac, ad, bc, and bd.
steps: Imagine you are designing a rectangular garden plot for your school
The length is (x + 3) metres and the breadth is (x + 5) metres
You want to find the total area without multiplying the binomials directly
Start by drawing a rectangle and splitting its length into x and 3, and its breadth into x and 5
This creates four smaller rectangles
Recall from Class 6 (c6_math_ch08_087) that area of a rectangle is length × breadth
cards.misconception: A wrong answer like "ac + bd" reveals the student thinks only the diagonal rectangles matter, missing the cross terms ad and bc. This shows they do not yet grasp that the whole rectangle's area is the sum of ALL four parts.
remember: What is the algebraic expression for the total area of a rectangle divided into four smaller rectangles with dimensions a × c, a × d, b × c, and b × d.
Explain why the area model for (x - 2)(x + 4) must include a region with negative area, and how that region is represented geometrically.
Use an area model to expand (2y + 3)(y - 4). Show all four sub-rectangles and write the final simplified expression.

cards.title: Applications of algebraic identities involve recognizing algebraic expressions…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: Applications of algebraic identities involve recognizing algebraic expressions that match the patterns of standard identities — (a+b)² = a² + 2ab + b², (a-b)² = a² - 2ab + b², and (a+b)(a-b) = a² - b² — and rewriting them in expanded or factored form to simplify calculations efficiently.
steps: Imagine you are tiling a square floor whose side length is (2x + 3) metres
To find the area, you could multiply (2x+3) by itself using the distributive property, but that takes several steps
Instead, you notice the expression matches the pattern (a+b)²
First, write down the area expression: (2x+3)²
Next, recall the identity (a+b)² = a² + 2ab + b²
Identify a = 2x and b = 3
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., missing the middle term 2ab, or writing (a+b)(a-b) = a² + b²) reveals that the student has not memorized the exact structure of each identity and may confuse the signs or the presence of the middle term.
remember: Write down the three standard algebraic identities for (a+b)², (a-b)², and (a+b)(a-b).
Explain why (a+b)² is not equal to a² + b². Use a numerical example with a=2, b=3 to support your explanation.
Simplify (3x - 4y)² using the appropriate identity. Show all steps.

cards.title: The distributive property of multiplication over addition states that…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: The distributive property of multiplication over addition states that multiplying a sum by a number gives the same result as multiplying each addend by the number and then adding the products. For any three numbers, variables, or algebraic expressions \(a\), \(b\), and \(c\), the expansion is \((a + b) \times c = a \times c + b \times c\). This rule allows us to remove brackets by distributing the multiplier \(c\) to each term inside the parentheses.
steps: Imagine you are buying stationery for your class: each student needs 1 pen (costing ₹\(a\)) and 1 notebook (costing ₹\(b\))
If there are \(c\) students, the total cost is \(c \times (a + b)\)

You can calculate this by finding the cost per student \((a+b)\) and multiplying by \(c\), OR by finding the total cost of all pens \((c \times a)\) and all notebooks \((c \times b)\) separately and adding them
This is exactly the distributive property you used in Class 7 arithmetic (c7_math_ch02_006) with numbers like \(5 \times (3+2)\)
Now, we apply it to algebraic terms
Write the expression \((a+b)c\)
cards.misconception: A wrong answer like \(xz + y\) or \(x + yz\) reveals the student does not understand that the multiplier \(z\) must be applied to both terms inside the bracket, a classic "incomplete distribution…
remember: State the algebraic rule for expanding \((x + y) \times z\). Write the expanded form without using brackets.
Explain why \(4 \times (5 + 3)\) and \(4 \times 5 + 4 \times 3\) give the same result. Use the meaning of multiplication as repeated addition in your explanation.
Expand and simplify: \((2p + 7q) \times (-3r)\). Show each step clearly.

cards.title: When one factor in a multiplication is increased by 1…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: When one factor in a multiplication is increased by 1, the product increases exactly by the value of the other factor. For any two numbers \(a\) and \(b\), \((a+1) \times b = a \times b + b\) and \(a \times (b+1) = a \times b + a\).
steps: Imagine you are buying notebooks for your class
Each notebook costs ₹15
You initially plan to buy 12 notebooks, so the total cost is \(12 \times 15 = ₹180\)
At the last moment, one more student joins, so you need 13 notebooks
How much extra money do you need? Instead of calculating \(13 \times 15\) from scratch, think: the new total is \((12+1) \times 15\)
Using the distributive property, this equals \(12 \times 15 + 1 \times 15 = 180 + 15 = ₹195\)
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., "increases by 1" or "increases by \(a\)") reveals the student thinks the increment transfers directly to the product or confuses which factor is…
remember: State the rule: If we have a product \(a \times b\) and we increase \(a\) by 1, by how much does the product increase? Write the new product in terms of the original product.
Explain why \((25 \times 37) + 37\) is equal to \(26 \times 37\) without calculating the actual products. Use the distributive property in your explanation.
If \(48 \times 12 = 576\), what is \(48 \times 13\)? Solve using the increment rule, showing your steps.

cards.title: Expanding (a + 1)(b + 1) means applying the distributive property twice…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: Expanding (a + 1)(b + 1) means applying the distributive property twice: each term in the first bracket multiplies each term in the second bracket, resulting in ab + a + b + 1. This is a special case of binomial expansion where both binomials have a constant term of 1.
steps: Imagine you're at a stationery shop buying notebooks
One notebook costs ₹a and you buy 1 extra pen for ₹1
Your friend buys notebooks at ₹b each and also 1 extra pen for ₹1
The total cost for both of you together is (a+1)(b+1)
To find this without multiplying directly, we distribute: first multiply a by (b+1), then multiply 1 by (b+1)
This connects to c8_math_ch6_1 where we learned a(b+c) = ab + ac
cards.misconception: A wrong answer like xy + 1 reveals the student thinks only the first terms multiply and the 1's multiply, missing the cross terms. This shows they are treating it like (a)(b) instead of distributing fully.
remember: Write the expansion of (x + 1)(y + 1) using the distributive property. Do not simplify.
Explain why (5 + 1)(7 + 1) = 5×7 + 5 + 7 + 1. Use the distributive property in your explanation.
Expand (2m + 1)(3n + 1) completely. Show each distribution step.

cards.title: When one factor in a product is increased by 1 and the other factor is…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: When one factor in a product is increased by 1 and the other factor is decreased by 1, the new product equals the original product plus the difference between the original factors minus 1. Mathematically, for any two numbers a and b: (a + 1)(b - 1) = ab + (b - a) - 1.
steps: Imagine you are buying notebooks: if each notebook costs ₹15 and you buy 12 notebooks, the total is ₹180
Now suppose the price increases by ₹1 (₹16) but you buy one less notebook (11)
Will you pay more or less? To find out, we use the distributive property we learned in c8_math_ch6_1 and c8_math_ch6_2
First, write the original product as a × b
Then write the new product as (a+1)(b-1)
Expand this using the distributive property: (a+1)(b-1) = a(b-1) + 1(b-1) = ab - a + b - 1
cards.misconception: A wrong answer like xy - 1 reveals the student forgot to distribute both terms and missed the -x + y part, treating it as a simple difference of squares pattern incorrectly.
remember: What is the algebraic expansion of (x + 1)(y - 1) using the distributive property.
If we have two numbers where the first number is larger than the second (a > b), and we increase the first by 1 while decreasing the second by 1, will the product increase….
The product of two numbers is 72. One number is 8 and the other is 9. If we increase 8 by 1 and decrease 9 by 1, what is the new product? Show your steps.

cards.title: The distributive property of multiplication over addition (and subtraction)…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: The distributive property of multiplication over addition (and subtraction) holds for all integers, including negative integers: for any integers \(a\), \(b\), and \(c\), \(a(b + c) = ab + ac\) and \(a(b - c) = ab - ac\). This means multiplying a negative integer by a sum (or difference) is equivalent to multiplying the negative integer by each term inside the bracket and then adding (or subtracting) the results, following the sign rules for integer multiplication.
steps: Imagine you owe your friend ₹5 for each of the 3 samosas you ate, and you also owe ₹2 for a chutney
Your total debt can be written as \(-5 \times 3 + (-2)\) or as \(-5(3) + (-2)\)
But what if you want to combine the costs first? You could think: "Each samosa with chutney costs ₹5 + ₹2 = ₹7, and I ate 3 sets, so my debt is \(-3 \times 7\)"
This is the distributive property with negatives: \(-3(5 + 2) = -3 \times 5 + (-3) \times 2\)
Start by identifying the integer outside the bracket and the terms inside (treating subtraction as adding a negative)
Multiply the outside integer by each term inside separately, carefully applying the sign rules: negative × positive = negative, negative × negative = positive
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., writing \(a(b + c) = ab + c\) or forgetting the subtraction version) reveals the student has memorized a pattern without understanding the structure, or does not recognize that subtraction is addition of a negative and the property…
remember: State the distributive property of multiplication over addition for integers \(a\), \(b\), and \(c\). Then write the version for subtraction.
Explain why \(-4 \times (6 - 3)\) equals \((-4 \times 6) - (-4 \times 3)\) using the concept of multiplication as repeated addition or a number….
Expand and simplify: \(-7(2x - 5y) + 3(-x + 4y)\).

cards.title: The algebraic identity \((a + b)^2 = a^2 + 2ab + b^2\) states that the square…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: The algebraic identity \((a + b)^2 = a^2 + 2ab + b^2\) states that the square of the sum of two terms equals the square of the first term, plus twice the product of the two terms, plus the square of the second term. This holds for all real numbers \(a\) and \(b\), including integers, fractions, decimals, and algebraic expressions.
steps: Imagine a square garden plot with side length \((x + 3)\) metres
To find its area, we could multiply \((x + 3)(x + 3)\)
Start by drawing a square split into four rectangles: an \(x \times x\) square, two \(x \times 3\) rectangles, and a \(3 \times 3\) square
This visual connects to the distributive property: \((x + 3)(x + 3) = x(x + 3) + 3(x + 3)\)
Expand each part: \(x^2 + 3x + 3x + 9 = x^2 + 6x + 9\)
Notice the middle term is twice the product of \(x\) and \(3\)
cards.misconception: A wrong answer like \(p^2 + 25\) reveals the student forgot the middle term \(2ab\). An answer like \(p^2 + 5p + 25\) shows they used \(ab\) instead of \(2ab\), indicating they don't realise the two cross terms are identical and must be added.
remember: Write the expansion of \((p + 5)^2\) using the algebraic identity.
Explain why \((2x + 3y)^2\) is not equal to \(4x^2 + 9y^2\). Use the distributive property in your explanation.
Expand \((3m - 4n)^2\) using the identity. Show all steps.

cards.title: The algebraic identity \((a + b)(a - b) = a^2…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: The algebraic identity \((a + b)(a - b) = a^2 - b^2\) states that the product of the sum and difference of the same two terms equals the difference of their squares. It holds for any real numbers or algebraic expressions \(a\) and \(b\).
steps: Imagine a rectangular garden where the length is 5 metres more than a side \(x\) and the breadth is 5 metres less than the same side \(x\)
The area is \((x+5)(x-5)\)
Instead of multiplying term-by-term, notice that the middle terms \(+5x\) and \(-5x\) cancel out, leaving only \(x^2 - 25\)
This pattern occurs whenever we multiply a sum by a difference of the same two terms
We first write the two binomials, identify \(a\) and \(b\), then directly write \(a^2 - b^2\)
This connects to the distributive property (c8_math_ch6_1) where we saw cross terms cancel when signs are opposite.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer like \((a+b)(a-b)=a^2+b^2\) reveals the student confuses this with the square of a sum and does not understand the cancellation of the middle terms.
remember: State the algebraic identity for the product of \((a + b)\) and \((a - b)\).
Explain why the middle terms cancel out when expanding \((a + b)(a - b)\) using the distributive property.
Use the identity to find the product \((2x + 3)(2x - 3)\) and then evaluate it for \(x = 4\).

cards.title: The algebraic identity \((a - b)(a - b) = a^2…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: The algebraic identity \((a - b)(a - b) = a^2 - 2ab + b^2\) states that the square of the difference of two terms equals the square of the first term minus twice the product of the two terms plus the square of the second term. It holds for all real numbers \(a\) and \(b\), and is derived by applying the distributive property twice: \((a - b)(a - b) = a(a - b) - b(a - b)\).
steps: Imagine you are tiling a square floor of side \((x - 3)\) metres
To find the area, you need to multiply \((x - 3)\) by itself
You already know how to expand \((a + b)^2\) from the previous lesson
Now, think of subtraction as adding a negative: \((x - 3) = (x + (-3))\)
Write down \((x + (-3))(x + (-3))\) and apply the distributive property step by step: first multiply \(x\) by each term in the second bracket, then multiply \(-3\) by each term
Combine like terms carefully, remembering that \((-3) \times (-3) = +9\)
cards.misconception: A wrong answer like \(4y^2 - 10y + 25\) reveals the student forgot to double the product \(ab\) (they computed \(ab\) instead of…
remember: Write the expansion of \((2y - 5)^2\) using the identity \((a - b)^2 = a^2 - 2ab + b^2\). Identify \(a\) and \(b\) clearly.
Explain why \((a - b)^2\) is NOT equal to \(a^2 - b^2\). Use the distributive property to show the missing term.
Expand and simplify: \((3x - 4y)^2 - (3x + 4y)^2\).

cards.title: Proportional change refers to a change where quantities vary in a constant…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: Proportional change refers to a change where quantities vary in a constant ratio. Multiplicative change scales a quantity by a factor (e.g., doubling, tripling, or multiplying by a fraction), preserving the ratio between related quantities. Additive change increases or decreases a quantity by a fixed amount (e.g., adding 5 or subtracting 3), which alters the ratio between related quantities unless all quantities change by the same absolute amount.
steps: Imagine you are helping your mother adjust a recipe for aloo paratha filling
The original recipe uses 2 cups of mashed potatoes and 1 cup of chopped onions for 4 parathas
She wants to make 8 parathas
A struggling student might say "add 2 cups potatoes and 1 cup onions" (additive), but that would change the…
Connect this to Class 6 ratio concepts (c6_math_ch06_062) where equivalent ratios are formed by multiplying both terms by the same number
The key insight: proportional situations require multiplicative thinking
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., "both preserve the ratio") reveals the student confuses absolute and relative change, a core misconception in proportional reasoning.
remember: State the fundamental difference between a multiplicative change and an additive change applied to two quantities that are in a ratio.
A rectangle has length 12 cm and breadth 8….
A map scale is 1 cm : 5 km.….

cards.title: When an image is scaled (enlarged or reduced)…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: When an image is scaled (enlarged or reduced), its width-to-height ratio (aspect ratio) remains constant if and only if the scaled image is similar to the original. Similar figures have corresponding angles equal and corresponding sides in proportion; the scale factor is the constant multiplier that relates every dimension of the original to the corresponding dimension of the scaled image.
steps: Imagine you have a photograph that is 12 cm wide and 8 cm tall, and you want to print a larger version that is 30 cm wide for a school exhibition

If you simply add 18 cm to both dimensions, the new photo would be 30 cm by 26 cm — does it look the same shape? No, because the original ratio 12:8 simplifies to 3:2, while 30:26 simplifies to 15:13, which is not equal
To keep the image looking identical (similar), you must multiply both dimensions by the same scale factor
Here the scale factor is 30 ÷ 12 = 2.5, so the new height must be 8 × 2.5 = 20 cm
This connects directly to the proportional reasoning you learned in c8_math_ch7_5 and c8_math_ch7_7: the two ratios form a proportion 12/8 = 30/h, which you can solve by cross-multiplication
The key insight is that similarity is preserved only by multiplicative scaling, never by additive changes.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer like 18:12 (not simplified) reveals the student does not recall that ratios must be expressed in simplest form (c8_math_ch7_3). An answer of 2:3 reveals confusion between width-to-height and height-to-width order.
remember: A rectangular image has width 18 cm and height 12 cm. What is its width-to-height ratio in simplest form.
Riya has a 10 cm × 6 cm photo.….
A movie poster is 60 cm wide and 90 cm tall.….

cards.title: A ratio is a comparison of two quantities of the same kind and in the same…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: A ratio is a comparison of two quantities of the same kind and in the same units, expressed as an ordered pair \(a : b\) (read as "a is to b") where \(a\) is the antecedent and \(b\) is the consequent. It represents the multiplicative relationship \(a/b\) and indicates how many times the first quantity contains the second.
steps: Imagine you are comparing the price of two notebooks: one costs ₹40 and the other ₹60
You could say the second is ₹20 more (additive), but in proportional reasoning we ask "how many times?" – the second costs 1.5 times the first
This multiplicative comparison is a ratio
Start by writing the two quantities with units: 40 rupees and 60 rupees
Check they are the same unit (yes, both rupees)
Write the ratio as 40:60, naming 40 the antecedent and 60 the consequent
cards.misconception: A wrong answer of 75:1.5 reveals the student ignores the unit requirement and compares numbers directly without conversion. A wrong answer of 1.5:75 shows confusion about order (antecedent vs consequent) or part-whole vs part-part thinking.
remember: Write the ratio of 75 cm to 1.5 m in the form \(a:b\). Do not simplify.
In a class of 40 students, 25 are girls. A student writes the ratio of girls to boys as 25:40. Is this correct? Explain why or why not.
A recipe uses 3 cups of flour and 2 cups of….

cards.title: A ratio a:b is in its simplest form when the two terms a and b have no common…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: A ratio a:b is in its simplest form when the two terms a and b have no common factor other than 1 (i.e., their highest common factor, HCF, is 1). To reduce a ratio to its simplest form, divide both terms by their HCF.
steps: Imagine Riya has 24 red marbles and 36 blue marbles
She wants to express the ratio of red to blue marbles in the simplest way possible
How can she do that? Connect this to the Class 7 idea of simplifying fractions by dividing numerator and denominator by their HCF
Explain that a ratio behaves exactly like a fraction: dividing both terms by the same non-zero number does not change the ratio
The key insight is that the simplest form is reached when the HCF of the two terms becomes 1
Show step-by-step: find HCF of 24 and 36 (which is 12), divide both by 12 to get 2:3.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., "when a and b are prime numbers") reveals confusion between prime numbers and co-prime numbers; the terms need not be prime, only co-prime.
remember: What is the condition for a ratio a:b to be in its simplest form.
Why does dividing both terms of a ratio by the same non-zero number not change the ratio? Explain using the concept of equivalent fractions.
Reduce the ratio 48:72 to its simplest form. Show all steps including finding the HCF.

cards.title: Two ratios a:b and c:d are equivalent if there exists a non-zero number k such…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: Two ratios a:b and c:d are equivalent if there exists a non-zero number k such that c = a × k and d = b × k, or c = a ÷ k and d = b ÷ k. Multiplying or dividing both terms of a ratio by the same non-zero number produces an equivalent ratio that represents the same multiplicative relationship between the quantities.
steps: Imagine you're helping your mother adjust a recipe for 4 people to serve 10 guests at a Diwali party
The original recipe uses 2 cups of rice and 3 cups of water — a 2:3 ratio
To scale up, you need to multiply both quantities by the same factor
If you only multiply the rice but not the water, the rice will be undercooked or mushy
This is why equivalent ratios require multiplying or dividing BOTH terms by the same number — it preserves the relationship
We already know from Class 6 that equivalent fractions work the same way (c6_math_ch03_031)
cards.misconception: A wrong answer like 20:7 or 5:28 reveals the student multiplied only one term instead of both, showing they don't understand that the multiplicative relationship between the two quantities must be preserved.
remember: What is the equivalent ratio of 5:7 when both terms are multiplied by 4.
Explain why the ratio 12:18 is equivalent to 2:3, but 12:18 is NOT equivalent to 4:5.
A map scale shows 1 cm represents 5 km. If two cities are 3.5 cm apart on the map, what is the actual distance between them? Show your working using equivalent ratios.

cards.title: A proportional relationship exists between two quantities when their ratio…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: A proportional relationship exists between two quantities when their ratio remains constant across all pairs of corresponding values, meaning one quantity is a constant multiple of the other (y = kx, where k is the constant of proportionality). This constant ratio must hold for every pair in the data set, not just for a single pair.
steps: Imagine you are buying mangoes at a fruit stall in Mumbai
The vendor sells them at ₹80 per kilogram
If you buy 1 kg, you pay ₹80
2 kg costs ₹160
3 kg costs ₹240
Notice how the cost increases by the same factor as the weight? Now consider an auto-rickshaw fare: ₹25 for the first kilometre plus ₹12 for each additional kilometre
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., "y increases when x increases" or "the difference y-x is constant") reveals the student confuses proportionality with general increasing relationships or additive change, missing the multiplicative constant-ratio requirement.
remember: State the mathematical condition that must be true for two quantities x and y to be in a proportional relationship.
A student claims that the relationship shown in the table below is proportional because "as x increases, y increases." Is the student….
The table shows the number of hours worked and total earnings for a part-time….

cards.title: The unitary method is a technique for solving proportional problems by first…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: The unitary method is a technique for solving proportional problems by first finding the value of a single unit from the given value of multiple units, then scaling that unit value to find the value of any desired number of units. It relies on the principle that in a direct proportion, the ratio between quantities remains constant.
steps: Imagine you are at a vegetable market in Delhi: 3.5 kg of tomatoes cost ₹105
Your mother asks you to buy 2.25 kg
How much will it cost? Start by writing down what you know: 3.5 kg → ₹105
To find the cost of 1 kg, you must divide the total cost by the total weight
This connects to the ratio concept from c8_math_ch7_2 where 3.5:105 simplifies to 1:30
Once you have the cost per kg (₹30), multiply by 2.25 kg to get the answer
cards.misconception: A wrong answer like "multiply 75 by 8" reveals the student does not understand that the unit value must be found first before scaling, confusing the unitary method with direct multiplication.
remember: What is the first step in the unitary method when you are given the total cost of 5 pens as ₹75 and asked to find the cost of 8 pens.
Explain why dividing the total quantity by the number of units gives the correct value for one unit in a direct proportion situation.
A car travels 180 km on 12 litres of petrol. How far can it travel on 15.5 litres? Show your working using the unitary method.

cards.title: Cross-multiplication is an algebraic method for solving a proportion of the…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: Cross-multiplication is an algebraic method for solving a proportion of the form \( \frac{a}{b} = \frac{c}{d} \) (where \( b \neq 0, d \neq 0 \)) by multiplying the numerator of each fraction by the denominator of the other, yielding the equation \( a \times d = b \times c \). This transforms the proportion into a linear equation that can be solved for an unknown variable.
steps: Imagine you are helping your mother adjust a recipe for 6 people that originally serves 4 people
The recipe needs 2 cups of flour for 4 servings
How much flour for 6 servings? You know the ratio of flour to servings stays constant, so you write \( \frac{2}{4} = \frac{x}{6} \)
Instead of finding the unit rate (flour per serving) as in the unitary method, we can directly cross-multiply: \( 2 \times 6 = 4 \times x \)
This gives \( 12 = 4x \), so \( x = 3 \) cups
Cross-multiplication works because if two fractions are equal, their cross-products are equal — a property derived from multiplying both sides of the equation by the common denominator \( bd \)
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., writing \( a \times b = c \times d \) or \( a \times c = b \times d \)) reveals the student does not understand which terms to multiply diagonally and is likely memorising a pattern without grasping the "cross" structure.
remember: State the cross-multiplication rule for the proportion \( \frac{a}{b} = \frac{c}{d} \) and write the resulting equation.
Explain why cross-multiplication is a valid step when solving \( \frac{3}{5} = \frac{x}{15} \). Use the concept of multiplying both sides by the same quantity.
Solve for \( x \) using cross-multiplication: \( \frac{7}{x} = \frac{21}{36} \). Show all steps.

cards.title: Two quantities are in direct proportion if they increase or decrease together…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: Two quantities are in direct proportion if they increase or decrease together in such a way that the ratio of their corresponding values remains constant. Mathematically, if quantity \(y\) is directly proportional to quantity \(x\), then \(\frac{y}{x} = k\) (a constant) or equivalently \(y = kx\), where \(k\) is called the constant of proportionality.
steps: Imagine you go to a fruit market where apples cost ₹60 per kilogram
If you buy 1 kg, you pay ₹60
2 kg costs ₹120
3 kg costs ₹180
Notice that as the weight increases, the cost increases in exactly the same proportion — the ratio of cost to weight is always 60
This is the essence of direct proportion: two quantities change together so that their ratio stays fixed
cards.misconception: A wrong answer like "\(x + y = \text{constant}\)" or "\(y = k + x\)" reveals the student confuses direct proportion with additive relationships or inverse…
remember: State the mathematical condition for two quantities \(x\) and \(y\) to be in direct proportion. Write the equation that relates them using a constant \(k\).
The table below shows values of \(x\) and….
The cost of 5 metres of cloth is ₹375.….

cards.title: Direct proportion describes a relationship between two quantities where an…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: Direct proportion describes a relationship between two quantities where an increase (or decrease) in one quantity causes a proportional increase (or decrease) in the other, such that their ratio remains constant. If quantity x and quantity y are in direct proportion, then x/y = k (a constant) or equivalently x = k × y.
steps: Imagine you are planning a class trip: 24 students need 6 litres of juice
How many litres are needed for 40 students? Start by asking: "Does the amount of juice increase or decrease when more students come?" Since more students need more juice, it is direct proportion
Write down the known ratio: 24 students : 6 litres
Connect this to the unitary method learned earlier (c8_math_ch7_6): find juice for 1 student, then multiply by 40
Alternatively, set up the proportion 24/6 = 40/x
The key insight is that the ratio students/juice stays constant, so we can equate ratios or use the constant of proportionality (k = 1/4 litre per student).
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., ₹625 by multiplying) reveals the student does not recall that the unitary method requires finding the value for ONE unit first by dividing, not…
remember: If 5 kg of wheat costs ₹125, what is the cost of 1 kg of wheat? (Recall the unitary method step for direct proportion.).
A car travels 60 km in 1 hour at constant….
A recipe uses 3 cups of flour for 12 cookies. How many cups of flour are needed for 30 cookies? Solve using the proportion method.

cards.title: Percentage is a way of expressing a number as a fraction of 100.
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: Percentage is a way of expressing a number as a fraction of 100. The symbol % means "per hundred", so x% = x/100. It represents a part-to-whole relationship where the whole is always considered as 100 equal parts.
steps: Imagine you and your friend take different tests: you score 36 out of 50, your friend scores 72 out of 100
Who did better? Comparing 36/50 and 72/100 directly is hard because the wholes (50 vs 100) are different
But if we scale your score to a base of 100 — multiply numerator and denominator by 2 — you get 72/100
Now both scores are out of 100: you both got 72 per hundred
That "per hundred" is what percentage means
The % symbol is just shorthand for "divided by 100"
cards.misconception: A wrong answer like "% means divide by 10" or "% is just a label" reveals the student treats % as a decorative symbol rather than a mathematical operator meaning "out of 100".
remember: What does the symbol % mean? Write the meaning in words and as a mathematical expression.
A shopkeeper says, "This shirt has a 50% discount." A student says, "That means the price becomes half." Is the student….
In a class of 40 students, 30 are present today. What percentage of the class is present? Show your steps using the definition of percentage.

cards.title: Simple interest applications involve using the formula \(SI = \frac{P \times R…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: Simple interest applications involve using the formula \(SI = \frac{P \times R \times T}{100}\) to solve real-world financial problems where interest is calculated only on the original principal amount for the entire duration. In Class 8, this extends to finding any missing variable (P, R, T, or SI) when the other three are known, handling time periods expressed in months or days, and comparing different investment or loan options.
steps: Imagine your older sibling wants to buy a second-hand scooter for ₹45,000 but only has ₹30,000 saved
They plan to borrow the rest from a relative at 8% simple interest per year and repay in 18 months
How much extra will they pay? Start by identifying what is given: Principal = ₹15,000, Rate = 8%, Time = 18 months
Convert time to years (18/12 = 1.5 years) because the rate is per annum
Use the simple interest formula \(SI = \frac{P \times R \times T}{100}\)
Substitute values and compute step by step
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., writing \(SI = P \times R \times T\) without dividing by 100, or confusing R as a decimal) reveals the student has memorised the formula incorrectly or does not understand that R is a percentage.
remember: What is the formula for calculating simple interest, and what does each letter represent.
Why must time be converted to years when the interest rate is given as "per annum"? Explain with an example.
Ravi deposits ₹25,000 in a bank at 6% simple interest per annum. How much interest will he earn in 2 years and 6 months.

cards.title: Discount is a reduction offered on the marked price (list price) of an item…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: Discount is a reduction offered on the marked price (list price) of an item, expressed as a percentage of the marked price. The discount amount is calculated as (Discount Percentage × Marked Price) ÷ 100, and the selling price equals Marked Price minus Discount Amount.
steps: Imagine you go to a bookstore during a "Back to School" sale
A novel has a price tag of ₹250 (marked price), but the sign says "20% off"
You need to find how much you actually pay
Start by recalling that "percent" means "per hundred" (from c8_math_ch8_1)
The discount is 20 per hundred of the marked price
Write down: Marked Price = ₹250, Discount % = 20%
cards.misconception: A wrong answer like "Discount Amount = (Discount Percentage × Selling Price) ÷ 100" reveals the student thinks discount is calculated on the selling price, confusing it with profit/loss percentage which is on cost price.
remember: What is the formula to calculate the discount amount when the marked price and discount percentage are given.
A shirt has a marked price of ₹800 and is sold at a discount of….
A pair of shoes is marked at ₹1,200. During a sale, a discount of 25% is offered. Calculate the selling price of the shoes.

cards.title: Goods and Services Tax (GST) is a single indirect tax levied on the supply of…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: Goods and Services Tax (GST) is a single indirect tax levied on the supply of goods and services at each stage of the supply chain, calculated as a fixed percentage of the taxable value (selling price before tax). The GST amount is added to the taxable value to give the final price paid by the consumer.
steps: Imagine you buy a school bag priced at ₹800 and the bill shows ₹944
You wonder: "Where did the extra ₹144 come from?" That extra amount is GST
Start by writing the taxable price (₹800) and the GST rate (say 18%)
Recall from c8_math_ch8_4 that finding a percentage of a quantity means multiplying the quantity by the percentage divided by 100
Compute step by step: 18 × 8 = 144
cards.misconception: A wrong answer like "GST = Taxable Value × GST Rate" (without dividing by 100) reveals the student treats the percentage as a whole number instead of a fraction out of 100, a common error from not converting percentage to decimal/fraction first.
remember: What is the formula to calculate the GST amount when the taxable value and GST rate are given.
A shopkeeper sells a notebook for ₹50 (taxable value) and charges 12%….
A pair of shoes costs ₹1,200 before GST. If the GST rate is 18%, find the total amount the customer pays.

cards.title: Expressing a fraction as a percentage means converting the fraction to an…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: Expressing a fraction as a percentage means converting the fraction to an equivalent value out of 100 by multiplying the fraction by 100 and appending the percent symbol (%). For any fraction \(\frac{a}{b}\) where \(b \neq 0\), the percentage is \(\frac{a}{b} \times 100\%\).
steps: Imagine you scored 18 out of 25 in a math test, and your friend says she got 72%
Who did better? To compare, you need to express your score as a percentage
Recall from c8_math_ch8_1 that "percent" means "per hundred"
So we ask: if 25 marks is the whole, what would your score be out of 100? Write the fraction \(\frac{18}{25}\)
To change the denominator to 100, multiply by 100: \(\frac{18}{25} \times 100 = 18 \times 4 = 72\)
Add the % sign: 72%
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., \(\frac{a}{b} \times 10\) or \(\frac{a \times 100}{b}\) without the % sign) reveals the student has not memorized the exact conversion rule or confuses it with decimal conversion (where you multiply by 10, 100, etc., based on decimal…
remember: Write the formula to convert a fraction \(\frac{a}{b}\) into a percentage.
Why do we multiply a fraction by 100 to convert it to a percentage? Explain using the meaning of "per cent".
Convert \(\frac{3}{8}\) to a percentage.

cards.title: A percentage is a fraction with denominator 100.
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: A percentage is a fraction with denominator 100. To convert a percentage to a fraction, write the percentage as the numerator and 100 as the denominator, then simplify to lowest terms. To convert a percentage to a decimal, divide the percentage value by 100 (equivalently, shift the decimal point two places to the left).
steps: Imagine you scored 75% on a test and your friend asks what fraction of the marks you got
You know "percent" means "per hundred", so 75% is 75 out of 100
Write it as 75/100, then simplify by dividing numerator and denominator by 25 to get 3/4
For the decimal, since 75% = 75/100, you simply write 0.75 (two decimal places because denominator is 100)
The key insight: the % symbol is just a shorthand for "divided by 100", so conversion is always dividing by 100 and then simplifying if needed.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer like 40/100 without simplifying reveals the student doesn't know to reduce fractions. Writing 0.04 reveals they shift the decimal point incorrectly (dividing by 1000 instead of 100).
remember: Write 40% as a fraction in simplest form and as a decimal.
Explain why 125% converts to a fraction greater than 1 and a decimal greater than 1, while 50% converts to values less than 1.
Convert 37.5% to a fraction in simplest form and to a decimal. Show all steps.

cards.title: Finding the percentage of a given quantity means calculating the part of the…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: Finding the percentage of a given quantity means calculating the part of the quantity that corresponds to a given percentage value, using the relationship that "per cent" means "per hundred". Mathematically, it is expressed as: (Percentage/100) × Given Quantity.
steps: Imagine you have ₹500 as pocket money and you want to save 20% of it for a new book
How much money will you put aside? Start by writing down the total quantity (₹500) and the percentage (20%)
Recall from c8_math_ch8_3 that 20% is the same as the fraction 20/100 or the decimal 0.20
Now think: "of" in mathematics means multiplication, just like when we found 1/3 of 15 in Class 6 fractions
So we multiply 20/100 by 500
The key insight is that percentage is simply a fraction with denominator 100, and finding its value on a quantity is exactly the same as multiplying that fraction by the quantity.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer like 15 × 80 or 80/15 reveals the student does not understand that "per cent" means division by 100 and "of" means multiplication.
remember: What is the mathematical expression for finding 15% of 80 kg.
Why does multiplying by 0.25 give the same result as finding 25% of a number.
Calculate 12.5% of ₹400.

cards.title: Expressing one quantity as a percentage of another means finding what fraction…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: Expressing one quantity as a percentage of another means finding what fraction the first quantity is of the second, then converting that fraction to a percentage by multiplying by 100. Mathematically, if quantity A is part of quantity B, then A as a percentage of B = (A/B) × 100%, provided both quantities are in the same units and B ≠ 0.
steps: Imagine you scored 38 marks out of 50 in your Mathematics test, and your friend scored 45 out of 60 in Science
Who performed better? You cannot compare 38 and 45 directly because the total marks are different
To compare fairly, you need to express each score as a percentage of its total
Start by writing the fraction: your score is 38/50, your friend's is 45/60
This connects to what you learned in c8_math_ch8_2 (expressing fractions as percentages)
Multiply each fraction by 100% to get the percentage
cards.misconception: A wrong answer like (Q/P) × 100% reveals the student confuses which quantity is the part and which is the whole. A student writing just P/Q without ×100% shows they understand the fraction but not the conversion to percentage.
remember: What is the formula to express quantity P as a percentage of quantity Q.
Rahul says: "To find 25 as a percentage of 200, I divide 200 by 25 and multiply by 100." Is Rahul correct? Explain why or why not.
A water tank holds 500 litres. Currently it contains 325 litres. What percentage of the tank is filled? Show all steps.

cards.title: Percentage increase is the change in a quantity expressed as a percentage of…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: Percentage increase is the change in a quantity expressed as a percentage of the original value, calculated as ((New Value - Original Value) / Original Value) × 100. Percentage decrease is similarly ((Original Value - New Value) / Original Value) × 100. The base for comparison is always the original value before the change.
steps: Imagine the price of your favourite bicycle was ₹3,000 last year, but this year the same model costs ₹3,300
You want to know by what percentage the price has increased
First, identify the original value (₹3,000) and the new value (₹3,300)
The increase is the difference: ₹300
Since percentage change is always calculated relative to the original value, we write the increase as a fraction of the original: 300/3000
Convert this fraction to a percentage by multiplying by 100, giving 10%
cards.misconception: A wrong answer like ((N - O) / N) × 100 reveals the student incorrectly uses the new value as the base, a very common error. Another wrong answer might omit the multiplication by 100, showing they confuse the fraction with the percentage.
remember: What is the formula for calculating percentage increase when the original value is O and the new value is N.
The price of a notebook increased from ₹50 to ₹60. A student calculates the percentage increase as (10/60) × 100 = 16.67%. Is this correct? Explain why or why not.
The population of a town decreased from 25,000 to 22,500 in one year. Calculate the percentage decrease.

cards.title: Profit and loss are financial outcomes determined by comparing the Selling…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: Profit and loss are financial outcomes determined by comparing the Selling Price (SP) of an item with its Cost Price (CP). Profit occurs when SP > CP and equals SP - CP; Loss occurs when CP > SP and equals CP - SP. The basic formulas are: Profit = SP - CP (if positive), Loss = CP - SP (if positive), SP = CP + Profit, CP = SP - Profit.
steps: Imagine you buy a cricket bat for ₹800 and sell it to a friend for ₹950
Did you gain or lose money, and by how much? Start by writing down the Cost Price (CP = ₹800) and Selling Price (SP = ₹950)
Recall from Class 7 percentages (c8_math_ch8_1) that comparing two quantities requires a reference point
here CP is the reference
Since SP > CP, you made a profit
Apply the formula Profit = SP - CP = ₹950 - ₹800 = ₹150
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., Profit = CP - SP) reveals the student confuses the order of subtraction and does not understand that profit means gaining extra money beyond the cost.
remember: State the formula for calculating profit when Selling Price (SP) and Cost Price (CP) are given. Also define Cost Price.

cards.title: Profit percentage is the profit expressed as a percentage of the cost price…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: Profit percentage is the profit expressed as a percentage of the cost price, calculated as (Profit ÷ Cost Price) × 100. Loss percentage is the loss expressed as a percentage of the cost price, calculated as (Loss ÷ Cost Price) × 100. Both percentages are always calculated with respect to the cost price, never the selling price.
steps: Imagine you buy a cricket bat for ₹800 and sell it for ₹920
Did you make a profit? By how much percent? Start by identifying cost price (₹800) and selling price (₹920)
Since selling price > cost price, there is a profit of ₹120
Now, to express this profit as a percentage, we need a base – the cost price is the base because it's the amount you invested
Always write: Profit = SP – CP, then Profit% = (Profit/CP) × 100
cards.misconception: A wrong answer like using selling price as denominator reveals the student doesn't understand that percentage is always calculated on the investment (cost price).
remember: Write the formula for profit percentage and loss percentage. State clearly what each variable represents.

cards.title: Simple Interest is the extra money paid or earned on a principal amount for a…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: Simple Interest is the extra money paid or earned on a principal amount for a specific time period at a fixed rate, calculated only on the original principal using the formula SI = (P × R × T) / 100, where P is the principal, R is the annual rate of interest in percent, and T is the time in years.
steps: Imagine you deposit ₹5,000 in a bank that offers 6% interest per year
After 3 years, how much extra money will the bank give you? Start by writing down what you know: Principal = ₹5,000, Rate = 6% per year, Time = 3 years
Recall from Class 7 percentages (c8_math_ch8_1, c8_math_ch8_4) that "6% per year" means ₹6 interest for every ₹100 principal for one year
For ₹5,000, first find interest for one year: (5000 × 6) / 100 = ₹300
Since simple interest is the same every year, multiply by 3 years: ₹300 × 3 = ₹900
This leads to the general formula SI = (P × R × T) / 100, where multiplying by T accounts for the constant yearly interest over T years.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer like SI = P × R × T (missing division by 100) reveals the student treats the percentage rate as a decimal without conversion. Writing R as a decimal (e.g., 0.06) but still dividing by 100 shows confusion between percentage and decimal forms.

cards.title: Baudhayana's Sulba-Sutra describes a geometric method to construct a square…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: Baudhayana's Sulba-Sutra describes a geometric method to construct a square with exactly twice the area of a given square: the side of the new square equals the diagonal of the original square. If the original square has side length a, its diagonal is a√2, and the square on this diagonal has area (a√2)² = 2a², which is double the original area a².
steps: Imagine a farmer in ancient India has a square field of side 10 metres and wants to mark out a new square field with exactly double the area for a different crop
He only has a rope and stakes — no calculator, no formula sheet
Ask: "If you double the side to 20 metres, what happens to the area?" (It becomes 4 times, not 2 times)
Guide students to recall that area of a square = side² (c6_math_ch08_087)
Then suggest: "What if we use the diagonal of the original square as the side of the new square?" Have them draw a 10 cm square, measure its diagonal (≈14.1 cm), and compute the new area (≈200 cm²)
The key insight: the diagonal is the geometric mean that doubles the area — this is the Sulba-Sutra's brilliant rope-geometry discovery.
cards.misconception: A wrong answer of 10 cm reveals the student thinks doubling the side doubles the area (confusing linear and quadratic scaling). An answer of 7 cm without √2 suggests they measured but don't grasp the exact geometric relationship.

cards.title: The converse of the Baudhayana-Pythagoras theorem states that in any triangle…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: The converse of the Baudhayana-Pythagoras theorem states that in any triangle, if the square of the longest side is equal to the sum of the squares of the other two sides, then the triangle is a right-angled triangle with the right angle opposite the longest side.

The carpenter measures the two adjacent sides and the diagonal but doesn't have a protractor

The converse lets us work backwards: if the side lengths satisfy this relation, the angle must be 90 degrees
First, identify the longest side (the candidate hypotenuse)
Then square all three sides
cards.misconception: A wrong answer (e.g., checking \(5^2 + 13^2 = 12^2\)) reveals the student does not understand that the longest side must be identified as the hypotenuse before applying the converse.

cards.title: A square with double the area of a given square can be constructed by using the…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: A square with double the area of a given square can be constructed by using the diagonal of the original square as the side length of the new square. If the original square has side length \(s\), its diagonal is \(s\sqrt{2}\), and the square built on this diagonal has area \((s\sqrt{2})^2 = 2s^2\), exactly twice the original area.
steps: Imagine you are a temple architect in ancient India designing a fire altar
You have a square altar of side 4 metres, but the ritual requires a new square altar with exactly double the area
Using only a rope (compass) and a straightedge, how would you construct it? Begin by drawing the given square
Recall from Class 6 that the diagonal of a square splits it into two congruent right-angled isosceles triangles

Now, using the diagonal as a side, construct a new square by drawing perpendicular lines at each endpoint and marking off the diagonal length

cards.title: Halving a square is the geometric construction of a new square whose area is…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: Halving a square is the geometric construction of a new square whose area is exactly half the area of a given square. If the original square has side length \(a\), the constructed square has side length \(\frac{a}{\sqrt{2}}\) (or equivalently, half the diagonal of the original square), and its area is \(\frac{a^2}{2}\).
steps: Imagine you are a tile designer in Jaipur creating a pattern for a courtyard
You have a square marble slab of side 60 cm, but the design requires a smaller square of exactly half the area to fit into a corner
How do you determine the size of the smaller square without measuring tapes or calculators, using only a ruler and…
To halve, we reverse the logic
First, draw the given square and its diagonal
The diagonal splits the square into two right isosceles triangles

cards.title: In an isosceles right triangle, the two legs (sides forming the right angle)…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: In an isosceles right triangle, the two legs (sides forming the right angle) are equal in length. If each leg has length \(a\), the hypotenuse \(h\) is given by \(h = a\sqrt{2}\). This relationship arises because the square on the hypotenuse has an area equal to the sum of the areas of the squares on the two equal legs (\(a^2 + a^2 = 2a^2\)), so the side of that square (the hypotenuse) is \(\sqrt{2a^2} = a\sqrt{2}\).

Since the area of the square on the leg is \(a^2\), the area on the hypotenuse is \(2a^2\), so its side must be \(\sqrt{2a^2} = a\sqrt{2}\)

cards.title: The Baudhayana-Pythagoras Theorem states that in a right-angled triangle…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: The Baudhayana-Pythagoras Theorem states that in a right-angled triangle, the area of the square constructed on the hypotenuse (the side opposite the right angle) is equal to the sum of the areas of the squares constructed on the other two sides (the legs). If the legs have lengths \(a\) and \(b\) and the hypotenuse has length \(c\), then \(a^2 + b^2 = c^2\).

cards.title: A visual proof of the Pythagoras theorem using area demonstrates that in a…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: A visual proof of the Pythagoras theorem using area demonstrates that in a right-angled triangle, the area of the square constructed on the hypotenuse equals the sum of the areas of the squares constructed on the other two sides, by dissecting and rearranging geometric shapes without changing their total area.

cards.title: A Pythagorean triple is a set of three positive integers (a, b…
cards.subject: Maths
cards.definition: A Pythagorean triple is a set of three positive integers (a, b, c) that satisfy the Baudhayana-Pythagoras theorem: a² + b² = c², where c is the largest number (hypotenuse) and a, b are the two smaller numbers (legs). cards.title: A focused scientific question is a precise…
cards.subject: Physics
cards.definition: A focused scientific question is a precise, testable inquiry that identifies a specific relationship between variables and can be investigated through controlled observation or experiment. It narrows a broad curiosity into a form that defines what will be changed (independent variable), what will be measured (dependent variable), and what conditions will be kept constant.

Now we practice the next step: picking ONE factor to change (heat) and ONE to measure (time between whistles) while keeping water amount, cooker size, and lid weight constant
This variable isolation is the heart of a focused question.

cards.definition: Observation in science is the deliberate, systematic gathering of information about a phenomenon using senses or instruments, while experimentation is a controlled procedure designed to test a specific prediction by manipulating one factor at a time and measuring the outcome. cards.title: Recording and interpreting observations is the systematic process of…

cards.title: Iterative investigation is the scientific process of repeatedly refining an…
